title: Apple Brings Free AI Note-Taking to the Watch
ai_summary: Apple announced Siri Recap, an AI note-taker for the Apple Watch that listens and summarizes conversations for free, with no transcript or speaker ID. Granola beat Apple to the wrist by over a month, already shipping a full Watch app with transcripts and action items, while Siri Recap remains in beta.

title: AI notetakers at work could leave companies at risk for lawsuits
ai_summary: Attorney Brian McGinnis discusses privacy lawsuits against AI notetaking tools, citing cases against Otter, Fireflies, Microsoft Teams, and Granola. The suits allege unauthorized recording and use of biometric data, with potential outcomes requiring opt-in consent from all meeting participants. Businesses are advised to obtain written consent and implement internal policies to avoid legal risk.

title: Growing Line of Litigation Involving AI Note-Takers Exposes Risks

title: Takeaways from the California Lawsuit Agaist Granola AI Notetakin
ai_summary: A California federal lawsuit has been filed against AI notetaking provider Granola, alleging the company's software recorded meeting participants without notice or consent and used meeting contents by default for commercial purposes including AI model training. The complaint combines multiple privacy legal theories, including claims under the federal Electronic Communications Privacy Act and the California Invasion of Privacy Act. The case highlights growing regulatory and legal risks for companies deploying AI transcription tools, emphasizing that consent and transparency must be built into workflows rather than treated as an afterthought.

title: Granola lawsuit raises concerns over AI note-taking app privacy
ai_summary: A privacy lawsuit was filed July 30 in a US District Court for the Northern District of California against AI note-taking app maker Granola, alleging the company "purposefully" designed its software to record and transcribe workplace conversations without requiring disclosure to all participants, violating the California Invasion of Privacy Act. The class action complaint, brought by Florida resident Tarra Chamberlain, also claims Granola by default uses transcription data for commercial purposes including AI model training. The case follows a similar ongoing lawsuit against Otter.ai and highlights broader privacy concerns surrounding AI note-taking tools in enterprise environments.

title: The Wave Continues to Build
ai_summary: Two new privacy class action cases filed in late July 2026 demonstrate that AI-related wiretap litigation is accelerating and expanding into workplaces and restaurant telephone systems. In Chamberlain v. Granola, Inc., a plaintiff alleges the company's AI notetaking application secretly intercepted Microsoft Teams and Zoom communications without consent, advancing a novel theory against non-party class members. In Thompson v. SoundHound AI, Inc., a plaintiff alleges the company's restaurant phone AI intercepted calls before any human greeting, routing communications through SoundHound's servers for real-time transcription. Both cases raise novel legal questions around federal statutory claims and consent requirements that organizations deploying AI voice tools must consider.

title: Granola CEO Refuses Enterprise Surveillance Deals — AI Note
ai_summary: Granola CEO Chris Pedregal announced that the company has declined enterprise contracts requiring admin surveillance access to employee meeting notes, positioning individual ownership of data as a core product philosophy. This stance differentiates Granola from competitors like Fireflies, Otter, and Microsoft Copilot, which typically offer administrative oversight features for compliance and productivity tracking. The decision highlights a strategic tension between user privacy preferences and the procurement demands of enterprise buyers who often require such surveillance capabilities.

title: This AI notetaker won't sell surveillance to your boss
ai_summary: In a Platformer podcast interview, Chris Pedregal, co-founder and CEO of AI notetaker company Granola, discussed the company's privacy-first approach to workplace AI tools, including its decision to keep meeting notes private by default and refuse employer access to transcripts. The company, valued at $1.5 billion with approximately 70-80 employees, is researching automatic deletion of verbatim transcripts and developing enhanced transcripts designed for AI agents. Pedregal predicted that AI transcription will likely become the default in work meetings and expressed optimism about the broader AI revolution, describing current AI tools as only '5 percent' into the transformation of how people work.

title: Granola AI notepad launches on Apple Watch, bringing one-tap meeting notes to your wrist
ai_summary: AI note-taking startup Granola launched its meeting notepad app on Apple Watch on July 28, 2026, enabling users to capture and transcribe conversations with a single tap without needing a phone or laptop. The watchOS app records offline and syncs to the paired iPhone where AI processes audio into structured notes including highlights, decisions, and action items. The launch positions Granola in the growing market for discreet AI capture tools, following the company's prior unicorn milestone after a $125 million Series C led by Index Ventures.

title: AI Notetakers Have Reached the Wrist. Big Privacy Questions Are Now at Hand
ai_summary: Granola, an AI note-taking startup, launched a free Apple Watch app on Tuesday that lets workers record and transcribe workplace conversations from their wrists during meetings, conference sessions, and office interactions. title: Apple Watch just gained a brand-new app for AI meeting notes

title: Granola launches an Apple Watch app
